deep.reconstruction:
PURPOSE. The heading reads 'Berechnung meiner Jupitersbeob. vom 30 Jun. 1818 nach Bouvards Tafeln'. Gauss computes Jupiter's apparent geocentric ecliptic place for his own observation of 30 June 1818. He takes Jupiter's heliocentric place from Bouvard's 1808 tables, adds the Sun's place, and compares the result with the observed place. Bouvard's tables use the centesimal division of the circle, so the heliocentric work is done in grads and converted to sexagesimal degrees at the end.

1) TIME ARGUMENT.
- Observation time: 12h1'19.0".
- Subtract the light time 34'26.0" (it is recomputed later as 2066.6 s), giving 11h26'53".
- First route: subtract 30'25" (Göttingen–Paris) and add 12h, giving 22h56'28" = 22.9411 h = Jun 30.95588. The marginal note 'Ist hier Tagzeit gemeint/gesetzt?' apparently questions this 12h convention.
- Second route: 11h26'53" - 3'10" = 11h23'43" = 11h23.717' = 11.3953 h, so t = Jun 30 + 11.3953/24 = Jun 30.4748. The meaning of the 3'10" is not stated (possibly an equation-of-time or longitude term; my guess).
- The small multiplications at top centre (3695, 40765, 87786, 13168, ...) are unidentified auxiliary products.

2) PERTURBATION ARGUMENTS II–XV. Table arguments are added to their increments: 7919+251=8170, 8414+82=8496, 6337+333=6670, 4756+415=5171, 424+59=483, 326+92=418, 951+17=968, 216+83=299, 535+67=602, 120+117=237, 8+9=17, 48+36=84. Below them are the tabulated inequalities read off (32, 54, 86, 140, 12, 7, -8, -2, 15, 4, 11, 18, 1, ...).

3) HELIOCENTRIC LONGITUDE (grads).
- Mean longitude: L = 298.17664 + 16.81057 - 0.00408 = 314.98313; then +0.36687 gives 315.35000.
- Perihelion: 12.6787 + 0.00872 = 12.68742.
- Mean anomaly: M = 315.35000 - 12.68742 = 302.66258 g (= 272.40°).
- Equation of centre brings the longitude to 308.9963 (read as such), which is about -6.354 g relative to 315.35.
- Then -0.00358 gives 308.99273.
- Fourteen periodic inequalities (in units of 10^-4 g: 557.2, 52.1, 249.3, 39.6, 4.5, 59.6, 56.7, 60.4, 39.1, 28.6, 7.5, 0.9, 0.05, 3.6) sum to 0.115915, giving 309.10864. Adding +0.000011 gives 309.10875 g.
- Conversion: 309.10875 x 0.9 = 278.197875° = 278°11'52.35".
- Reduction to the ecliptic: -10.30", giving l = 278°11'42.05".

4) RADIUS VECTOR. 5.19753 + (555+18+176+280+13+23+13+8+22)·10^-5 = 5.20861.

5) LATITUDE.
- Node: 109.5423 + 0.00527 = 109.54757 g.
- Argument of latitude: u = 309.10864 - 109.54757 = 199.56107 g.
- Tabulated 99.98810 + corrections = 99.99103, i.e. b = (100 - 99.99103) g = 0.00897 g = +29.06".

6) SUN / EARTH.
- The Sun's daily motion 57'13.6" = 3433.6" is multiplied by 0.4748 day: 3433.6 x 0.4748 = 1630.27" = 27'10.27".
- Earth's heliocentric longitude: 278°26'16.77" + 20.62" = 278°26'37.39" (the 20.62" is presumably aberration).
- Earth minus Jupiter: 278°26'37.39" - 278°11'42.05" = 14'55.34". Jupiter is essentially at opposition.

7) GEOCENTRIC REDUCTION. Gauss writes (Δ = curtate distance, r' = curtate radius vector):
  Δ sin(λ' - l) = R sin(⊙ - l)
  Δ cos(λ' - l) = r' - R cos(⊙ - l)
  Δ tan β' = r tan b
In logarithms:
- log R = 0.0072410; log sin 14'55.34" = 7.6375614; log cos = 9.9999959.
- log R cos = 0.0072369; log R sin = 7.6448024.
- log r = 0.7167218.
- Gaussian subtraction-logarithm step: log(r/(R cos) - 1) = 0.6151643, so log(r - R cos) = 0.6224012 ≈ log Δ.
- Correction to longitude: λ' = l - 3'36.19" = 278°8'5.86".
- Latitude: log 29.06 = 1.46330, plus log(r/Δ) = 0.09432, gives 1.55762, so β' = 36.11".
- Light time: log Δ + log 493.0 s (0.69285) gives 2066.6 s = 34'26.6". This is the 34'26" used at the top.
- The entries 1.99813, 47.51", 1.67676, 96336, 51.69", 3.442" are further small auxiliary terms (light-time or motion corrections) that I cannot securely interpret.

8) SECOND (REVISED) PASS.
- New heliocentric values: l = 278°6'36.26", r = 5.20918, b = 36.92". The change of l by about 5'06" is about one day of Jupiter's motion; this looks like a corrected time argument (my inference).
- 278°26'37.39" - 278°6'36.26" = 20'1.13".
- log sin = 7.7651624; log cos = 9.9999926; log R cos = 0.0072336; log r = 0.7167693.
- Subtraction log: 0.6152279, so log Δ = 0.6224611; log R sin = 7.7724034.
- Latitude: log 36.92 (1.56726) + 0.09431 = 1.66157, so β' = 45.87".
- Longitude: Gauss subtracts 5'12.15", giving λ' = 278°1'24.11" (boxed), β' = +0°0'45.87".

9) OBSERVED PLACE. Observed RA 278°44'44.94" and Dec -23°12'23.79" are converted to ecliptic coordinates with an auxiliary angle N and obliquity 23°27'54.60":
- tan N = tan δ / sin α, with log tan δ = 9.6321911 and log sin α = 9.9949207, giving N ≈ 23°27'1.00".
- N - ε = 53.60" (log 1.72916). Times 9.9957172 gives β = 53.07".
- tan λ is obtained via 0.8129307 + 0.0374385.
- Result: λ = 278°1'59.91", β = +53.07".
Parallax in declination: log 8.6" = 0.93450, minus log Δ (0.66240 as written, i.e. 0.6224), gives 0.31210. Adding log sin(φ - δ) = 9.98441 (φ ≈ 51°32', δ ≈ -23°12') gives 1.98".

10) COMPARISON. Calc - Obs = 278°1'24.11" - 278°1'59.91" = -35.80" in longitude, and 45.87" - 53.07" = -7.20" in latitude. This is a check of Bouvard's tables against Gauss's own observation.
errors: Equation of centre: with M = 302.66258 g (272.40°) and e ≈ 0.0482, a Kepler-series estimate gives about -5.53° = -6.15 g. The page implies about -6.354 g from 315.35 (or -5.987 g from 314.98). This is either a misreading of the intermediate line or the table equation includes extra terms; it is not verified.
First pass: atan(10^(7.6448024-0.6224012-10)) = 217.18", but Gauss uses 3'36.19" = 216.19". This is a possible 1" slip, or a small additional correction that is not written.

Second pass: the logs on the page give atan(10^(7.7724034-0.6224611-10)) = 291.3" = 4'51.3". Gauss subtracts 5'12.15" = 312.15", which differs by about 20.8" (close to an aberration-size term). Either a correction not shown on the page or an error. If 4'51.3" is correct, the calculated λ would be 278°1'44.9" and Calc - Obs only about -15".
Argument VIII: 110 + 7 is written as 119. Either the increment is 9 or there is a misreading/slip.
The first time reduction (adding 12h to reach 22h56'28" = Jun 30.95588) appears to have been doubted by Gauss himself (marginal note) and replaced by Jun 30.4748.

results.what: Computation of Jupiter's heliocentric place from Bouvard's 1808 tables (centesimal), with mean longitude, equation of centre, 14 periodic inequalities, radius vector and latitude
Heliocentric-to-geocentric reduction Δ sin(λ'-l) = R sin(⊙-l), Δ cos(λ'-l) = r' - R cos(⊙-l), Δ tan β' = r tan b, evaluated with Gaussian subtraction logarithms
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (18th c.); Gaussian logarithm tables credited to Gauss/Leonelli

results.what: Light-time correction (Δ x 493 s = 2066.6 s subtracted from the observation time)
Conversion of observed RA/Dec to ecliptic λ, β via auxiliary angle N (tan N = tan δ / sin α)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine observatory reduction: a comparison of Gauss's 1818 Jupiter observation with Bouvard's tables using standard formulas and Gaussian logarithms. It is of archival interest only, for example for documenting a Jupiter observation and table error of about -36" in longitude.
transcription_corrections: '393.6463.1' in column 1 should read approximately '308.9963.1' (needed to give 308.9927.3 after -35.8).
'6mg40' is '66240' (log Δ ≈ 0.6224, as written by Gauss).
The symbol before '278 26 37 39' is the Earth/Sun sign (heliocentric Earth longitude), not ♄.
'Ist hier Tagzeit gemeint [?]' is probably 'Ist hier Tagzeit gesetzt?' (a query about the 12h day-reckoning).
'69285' is log 493.0 (light time for 1 AU in seconds), i.e. 2.69285.
